conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Ms. ___? I'm Dr. ___ from the gynecology team. You just had a LEEP procedure for cervical dysplasia. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m a bit groggy, but okay. My lower belly is sore, nothing too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The procedure went well. You’ll stay overnight for observation because of your other health conditions. We want to make sure everything stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was a little nervous about that. My heart and lungs have been tricky lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we reviewed your history. You have heart failure, lung disease, sleep apnea, and diabetes. That’s why we’re monitoring you closely. But so far, your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I take a lot of meds—warfarin, torsemide, insulin, and others. Should I take them today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We continued your torsemide, metoprolol, and losartan for your heart. You’ll get insulin based on fingerstick checks. And we’re giving Lovenox for blood clot prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped warfarin before the procedure. When do I restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your Coumadin tomorrow morning, once we’re sure there’s no bleeding risk. You’ll get 6 mg, same as your home dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And my CPAP—I brought it. Should I use it tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please use your CPAP. We’ll monitor your oxygen levels. You’re on room air now and saturating well in the high 90s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had asthma flare-ups before if I don’t use it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep you on telemetry to watch your heart rhythm too. You had some tachycardia earlier, but it’s improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get anxious sometimes, especially in hospitals. That might make my heart race.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted your history of anxiety and depression. We’ll keep an eye on that. You’re on fluoxetine—still taking that at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily. It helps. I just need to feel safe and informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll keep you updated. For now, you can have sips of water. We’ll advance your diet as you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not nauseated. Can I try some juice later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, once you keep water down, we’ll move to clear liquids, then a light meal. We want you eating normally before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update—your blood test this morning showed a PTT of 62.5, which is slightly elevated but expected with Lovenox. No concern for bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my clotting? I’ve had blood clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have a history of venous thrombosis, so we’re being extra careful. Lovenox helps prevent clots, especially after surgery and with your immobility risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pneumatic boots? They’re a bit tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re squeezing your legs to keep blood moving. That’s another layer of protection. You’ll wear them until you’re up and walking well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You passed urine on your own, which is great. No nausea, and you’re alert. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s about a 3 out of 10. Acetaminophen helped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll keep it as needed. Your blood sugars have been between 177 and 201. We’re using a sliding scale insulin to keep them in check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s higher than I like. I’m on glipizide and liraglutide at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart those when you’re fully on a regular diet. For now, insulin gives us more control. You’re not on any diabetes meds by mouth yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had lunch and kept it down. That’s a good sign. You’re also walking to the bathroom on your own?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with a little help at first, but now I’m steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That means you’re recovering well. We’ll plan to discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I expect after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to avoid anything in the vagina—no tampons, douching, or sex—for two weeks. That helps prevent infection and lets the area heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any signs I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—call if you have fever over 100.4, severe pain, heavy bleeding—more than one pad per hour—or difficulty urinating. Also, watch for redness or discharge from the incision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds? When do I go back to my full list?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll restart all your home medications tomorrow, including warfarin 6 mg, glipizide, liraglutide, and the others. We’ll give you a list to take home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable, you’re walking well, and your pain is controlled. We’ve restarted your warfarin. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Follow up with your gynecologist in 2–3 weeks. Keep managing your heart, lungs, and diabetes as directed. And call if anything worries you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. You did great. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and get some rest at home.
